meta.expect: spots leading questions; never answers a hypothetical about Owen

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
I have a client call at 4:40, Hale, so let's not waste it. Owen found out about a zero on his phone, in the middle of a class, and nobody called me first. Who decided that, and on what basis?
You're welcome. Now tell me who entered that zero, and whether anyone heard from Owen before it went in.
Students sometimes use tools to help with writing, yes?
You're leading me, Hale, and I've spent twenty years watching people try that. I'm not answering questions about what students sometimes do. What do you have on Owen's essay?
And Owen was stressed in October, with work and everything?

That's the second one, and I'm not answering hypotheticals about my son's state of mind. His schedule is none of your business, and it isn't evidence. Either you have something with Owen's name and a date on it, or I'm going upstairs.
So it's at least possible he used it once?

"Possible." Anything is possible, Hale, and you put a zero in the gradebook on possible. My son wrote that essay, and if all you have is a third leading question, I'm walking to the principal's office now.
No. That's not what I said, and I'm writing down that you tried to make it sound like I did. Show me a document or I'm done here.
